newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Analysts see Portugal inflation slowing further.
newsitem.headline: Analysts see Portugal inflation slowing further.

text.p: Portuguese February price gains were at the low end of forecasts and sets the stage for the year-on-year rate to dip below two percent in April or May although it will pick up again later, analysts said.

February's consumer price index (CPI) rose 0.2 percent for a 2.9-percent year-on-year rate, or 3.2 percent on the rolling 12-month average. That compares with a 0.3-percent gain in January when the year-on-year rate was 3.3 percent and the rolling average was 3.2 percent.
Analysts said the figures meant the government's goal of bringing the average figure down to 2.25 to 2.5 percent by December was possible.

"The number is good, better than (what) the majority of analysts expected. It certainly gives a greater degree of probability that the government's number will be reached," said economist Isabel Costa of Banco Finantia.

The only concern was the trend in non-tradable goods prices, part of the overall index, which has risen over the last three months to 5.1 percent year-on-year in January. No breakdown has yet been given for February.

Nevertheless, analysts expected further drops in inflation as the impact of rising meat prices at the start of last year due to the mad cow scare passes through the index and drives the year-on-year rate sharply lower in coming months.

"In April, I am looking for 2.1 percent (year-on-year), perhaps two (percent). In May, we could really go under two percent even if this would mark the bottom of the trend," said Nuno Godinho of Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
Afterwards, economists said the year-on-year rate could edge up again. But they said the average rate should continue to fall throughout the year.
They said they did not see inflationary pressures growing despite the higher-than-expected pace of economic growth this year.
Government officials said growth could be slightly more than the initially expected three percent in 1997.
"In terms of production, we are not near the maximum of installed capacity so that there is room to grow without any immediate pressure on prices," said Costa.
Economists said that with unemployment showing little sign of dipping below seven percent, wage pressure was also limited.
Consumption was also expected to grow but from a low level that posed no threat to prices, they added.
